lesson_title: Fusing On-Chain Findings with Other Sources

metadata.note: No assigned reading for this lesson; every question is grounded in a visible slide.

lectures.title: Fusing On-Chain Findings with Other Sources - lesson synthesis

questions.question_stem: Which of these questions can the chain answer by itself?
questions.correct_answer: What moved, when it moved and to which address it went.
incorrect_answers: Which service holds that address, as the ledger lists it.
Who controls the account, as the chain shows it all.
What the operators knew, as each transaction shows it.
questions.explanation: The lesson's table gives the chain what moved, when and where; who holds an address, who controls an account and what they knew come from sources off the chain.
questions.lesson_block: The chain says what moved; others say who

specific_source.anchor: The chain says what moved; others say who

questions.question_stem: An exchange publishes a list of its own wallets. What does that kind of source add?
questions.correct_answer: Who holds the exact address, but only for the wallets the owner chose to list.
incorrect_answers: Who sent funds to the address, because the list shows each depositor's full name.
Why the funds moved, because an owner explains every transfer it lists.
Which other exchanges hold the address, as rivals check each list for them all.
questions.explanation: An owner's list adds who holds the exact address. It covers only what the owner chose to list and is dated, as of 31 Oct 2026.
questions.lesson_block: Six kinds of source, and what each adds

specific_source.anchor: Six kinds of source, and what each adds

questions.question_stem: Which ICD 203 factor does the lesson tie to the question 'Could the subject have planted it?'
questions.correct_answer: Possible denial and deception, such as a fake identity or a borrowed alias.
incorrect_answers: Age and continued currency, since owners rotate wallets and drop them.
Source access and validation, since a source may only infer from behavior.
Motivation and possible bias, since a source may sell the label it gives.
questions.explanation: The judging table pairs possible denial and deception with the question of a planted fake identity or borrowed alias; the other factors ask about age, access and motive.
questions.lesson_block: Judge each source before you count it

questions.question_stem: An open label set is built from OFAC's published addresses and matches OFAC's list. How many lines is that?
questions.correct_answer: One; the set repeats OFAC's list, so the agreement is an echo.
incorrect_answers: Two; an independent project published it, so its agreement counts.
Two; the set was built later, so the later date adds a second line.
Zero; open label sets are never accepted as a source of evidence.
questions.explanation: The b10c set agrees with OFAC because it is OFAC. Count the origins, not the labels.
questions.lesson_block: An echo is not a second line

specific_source.anchor: An echo is not a second line

questions.question_stem: Three vendor tags all trace to one government release. How many lines is that, and what confidence?
questions.correct_answer: One strong line from the release, so Moderate and not High.
incorrect_answers: Three lines, so High, because three tags agree with one another.
Three lines, so Moderate, because the vendors differ in size.
One weak line, so Low, as tags never rest on a release.
questions.explanation: The callout reads: three tags that trace to one government release are one strong line: Moderate.
questions.lesson_block: An echo is not a second line

specific_source.anchor: An echo is not a second line

questions.question_stem: In the Exchange X example, a second vendor tags T-addr 'Exchange X', basis unknown. Where does the confidence word stand?
questions.correct_answer: Still Low, because it could be an echo and so still counts as one label.
incorrect_answers: Moderate, because two independent vendors now agree about the address.
High, because both vendors agree on the label and none disagrees.
Moderate, because a second vendor is a second line, whatever its basis is.
questions.explanation: Step 3 stays Low: the second tag could be an echo, so it is still one label.
questions.lesson_block: How each source moves the confidence word

specific_source.anchor: How each source moves the confidence word

questions.question_stem: In the Exchange X example, what moves the confidence word to High?
questions.correct_answer: Exchange X's own published list includes H, the wallet T-addr sweeps into.
incorrect_answers: A third vendor tags T-addr as Exchange X, and its basis is not stated.
The large daily USDT inflows from many senders keep growing over weeks.
Your trace shows T-addr sweeps its USDT into one wallet, H, each day.
questions.explanation: Steps 1 to 4 stay Low. Step 5, the owner's published list, is a new kind of line that agrees with the chain, with no known failure: High.

questions.question_stem: In the Bitfinex case, what did the account records add that the chain did not?
questions.correct_answer: Who opened the exchange accounts, some under fictitious identities.
incorrect_answers: Where the 119,754 BTC went after it left, as records follow each hop.
How many transactions the theft took, as only records count them.
Which wallets held the 95,000 BTC, as accounts name each wallet.
questions.explanation: The chain showed the 119,754 BTC leaving and the hops; the account records showed who opened the accounts, and some of them lied. The DOJ release is dated 3 August 2023.

questions.question_stem: A launderer's address shows an AddedBlackList event. What can the analyst state?
questions.correct_answer: It is blacklisted as of that date; the reason is only what was quoted.
incorrect_answers: It is blacklisted because OFAC named the owner, as the event records it.
It is blacklisted because Tether found the funds were stolen in a hack.
It is blacklisted, which shows a court ordered the freeze on that very day.
questions.explanation: The fact comes from the chain; the reason is a claim and is only what the issuer or the government said, quoted with its date.
questions.lesson_block: A freeze is a source: read it narrowly

specific_source.anchor: A freeze is a source: read it narrowly

questions.question_stem: On Tron, who can add an address to USDT's blacklist, and how can the analyst check it?
questions.correct_answer: The contract's owner, a multisig as of 31 Oct 2026; the AddedBlackList events show it.
incorrect_answers: Any exchange that holds USDT, and Tether then logs each request off chain in its own records.
Any holder of USDT, by a vote; the votes appear in the contract's token transfers.
Tron's validators, by a block rule; the results show in a block explorer's flags.
questions.explanation: USDT's Tron contract has addBlackList and emits AddedBlackList; the owner is a multisig, as of 31 Oct 2026, and the analyst can read who was frozen and when.

questions.question_stem: A vendor says T-addr is Exchange X, but Exchange X's own list does not include it. What does the lesson say to write?
questions.correct_answer: State both, take the lower confidence, and name what would settle it, such as T-addr sweeping into a listed wallet.
incorrect_answers: Prefer the owner's list and drop the vendor's tag, since an owner always knows its own wallets best of all.
Prefer the vendor's tag and call the list out of date, since lists always lag the market behind it every day.
Average the two sources and report Moderate, since one agrees with the claim and one disagrees with it here.
questions.explanation: Disagreement is information. The model assessment is Low that T-addr is Exchange X, rising if T-addr sweeps into a listed wallet.

questions.question_stem: A classified report names a Tron address. How does it enter an unclassified assessment?
questions.correct_answer: As one line, judged like any other; check if it echoes open reporting.
incorrect_answers: As a line that outweighs open sources, so the word rises to High at once.
As a line judged on a lower bar, since it needs no access checks at all.
As a line quoted word for word, since an assessment needs the full detail.
questions.explanation: A classified line gets the same questions, the same counting and the same words; an unclassified assessment rests only on lines its reader may see, and names the gap when it matters.

questions.question_stem: Vendor A tags T-practice 'OTC desk' with no basis. Vendor B tags it the same, and B's note cites A. How do you count them?
questions.correct_answer: As one line, because B's note cites A; the pair counts once.
incorrect_answers: As two lines, because the vendors are separate firms that publish.
As two lines, because B's note adds a second date to the tag.
As no line, because a tag with no basis is never counted.
questions.explanation: Vendor B's note cites Vendor A, so B is an echo and the pair is one line, which is weak because its basis is unstated.
